one_liner: Dense-prediction scaling laws diverge from classification: boundary quality scales with a smaller exponent than region accuracy - fit both.
problem: Scaling laws exist for classification/LLMs (KNOWN), but dense prediction may scale differently per output property: region-level semantics might follow data/model power laws while boundary precision saturates early (limited by resolution and label noise, not knowledge). No one has fitted property-resolved scaling curves.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: fitting scaling curves separately for region metrics and boundary metrics across model/data ladders reveals significantly different exponents (boundary exponent near zero beyond moderate scale - scale does not buy sharpness), implying the field's scaling investments improve WHAT models segment but not HOW WELL they trace it - a structural argument for redirecting boundary research away from scale.
why_important: Scaling strategy is the biggest resource decision in the field; property-resolved laws would show which problems scale can and cannot solve.
why_possibly_novel: Property-decomposed scaling analysis for segmentation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Train/collect model ladders (existing checkpoint series + controlled small-scale runs), fit region-vs-boundary scaling exponents with confidence intervals.
main_risk: Boundary metrics hit label-noise floors that masquerade as saturation; use metrology-grade evaluation subsets (see physical-GT benchmark idea).

one_liner: The probing atlas: layer-by-layer, which foundation models linearly encode boundaries, parts, materials, and occlusion - a standardized dense-knowledge inventory.
problem: Claims like 'DINOv2 knows objects' rest on scattered probes with incompatible protocols. The field lacks a standardized, property-resolved inventory of what dense information each foundation model encodes linearly, at which layer, at what spatial precision.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a standardized probing battery (boundaries, part hierarchies, material vs shape, occlusion ordering, metric size) across major foundations will reveal strongly model-family-specific knowledge profiles (contrastive models encode materials better; MAE-style encode layout better; SAM encodes boundary-ownership uniquely) that PREDICT downstream fine-tuning outcomes per task better than aggregate benchmark scores - knowledge profiles, not leaderboard positions, should drive backbone selection.
why_important: Backbone choice is every project's first decision, currently made by leaderboard folklore; a validated knowledge inventory would replace it with measurement.
why_possibly_novel: Standardized cross-foundation dense-probing with downstream-predictivity validation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Build the probe battery on 5 properties x 6 foundations x all layers, correlate profile-task match scores with realized fine-tuning outcomes on 8 tasks.
main_risk: Linear probes underestimate nonlinearly-encoded knowledge; include lightweight nonlinear probes as sensitivity analysis.

one_liner: Sub-patch information is not lost - it hides in neighboring tokens: measure recoverable sub-tokenization detail across ViT foundations.
problem: Patch tokenization (14-16px) supposedly destroys sub-patch spatial detail, capping dense tasks. But convolution-free ViTs may distribute sub-patch information across neighboring tokens' interactions - whether fine detail is destroyed or merely delocalized is a measurable representational question.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: sub-patch edge positions are decodable from local token NEIGHBORHOODS (not single tokens) at precision well below patch size (2-4px) in mid layers, decoding precision varies strongly across pretraining objectives, and the delocalized detail is exactly what boundary-refinement heads fail to exploit - foundation features contain more sharpness than any current decoder extracts.
why_important: If detail survives delocalized, boundary quality is a readout problem (fixable cheaply), not a representation problem (needing new pretraining) - a fork in the road for boundary research.
why_possibly_novel: Neighborhood-decoding analysis of sub-patch information is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Train sub-pixel edge-position probes on token neighborhoods across layers/models using synthetic exact-edge stimuli, map recoverable precision.
main_risk: Synthetic edges may over-estimate recoverability on natural texture; validate on the physical-GT benchmark stimuli.

one_liner: Attention-sink artifacts corrupt dense features in predictable spatial patterns: map the damage and its downstream cost per task.
problem: KNOWN: ViTs develop high-norm artifact tokens (Darcet et al., 'Vision Transformers Need Registers'). What remains unmeasured is the spatial structure of artifact damage in dense downstream tasks - where in the image artifacts land, which classes suffer, and how much performance the artifacts actually cost end-to-end.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: artifact tokens localize preferentially in low-information regions (sky, walls) but their attention distortion damages predictions in a measurable halo AROUND those regions (displaced errors), the per-task cost is significant for segmentation but negligible for classification (explaining why the problem went unnoticed), and artifact-location prediction enables test-time feature cleaning worth a consistent fraction of the gap to register-equipped models.
why_important: Quantifies a known pathology's real dense-task cost and offers retrofit mitigation for the enormous installed base of artifact-bearing checkpoints.
why_possibly_novel: Spatial damage-mapping and retrofit-cleaning accounting is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search (the artifact phenomenon itself is KNOWN).
minimal_experiment: Localize artifacts across images, correlate with spatial error maps on segmentation, implement cleaning, measure recovered performance vs register-model upper bound.
main_risk: Artifact behavior differs across model families; scope claims per family.

one_liner: Generative vs discriminative pretraining for boundaries: diffusion features encode edges sharper than contrastive features - a controlled spectral comparison.
problem: Diffusion models must synthesize exact boundaries (generation demands sharpness), while contrastive objectives reward invariance (blur tolerance). Whether generative pretraining therefore yields sharper dense features - controlled for data and scale - is a fundamental objective-level question tangled in uncontrolled comparisons.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: at matched data and compute, diffusion-pretrained features support higher boundary-precision readout (measurable via edge-position probing and boundary metrics) while contrastive features support better semantic discrimination - a principled objective-property tradeoff, implying optimal dense systems should read boundaries and semantics from DIFFERENT pretraining lineages.
why_important: Resolves a foundational which-objective-for-what question with design consequences for every dense pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: Matched-budget objective comparison focused on boundary spectra is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search (uncontrolled diffusion-feature studies are KNOWN to exist).
minimal_experiment: Pretrain matched mid-scale models (diffusion, contrastive, MAE) on identical data, run boundary-precision and semantic probes, compare property profiles.
main_risk: Matched-budget pretraining is expensive at meaningful scale; use the largest affordable scale with scaling-trend checks.

one_liner: What makes a good visual in-context example? Retrieval laws for one-shot segmentation prompting with image-mask pairs.
problem: Visual in-context segmentation (prompt with example image-mask pairs, e.g. SegGPT-style - KNOWN to exist) is acutely sensitive to support-example choice, but support selection is folk art; the quantitative laws (what similarity dimensions matter, how gains scale with support-set size and diversity) are unmapped.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: in-context segmentation quality is predicted by a learnable composite of support-query similarities where POSE and SCALE similarity dominate semantic similarity (opposite to text-LLM intuitions), gains saturate at very few supports (2-4) unless supports are diversity-selected, and a retrieval policy trained on these laws beats random/semantic retrieval by a large margin - in-context vision has its own retrieval science distinct from NLP's.
why_important: In-context dense models are the most annotation-efficient adaptation path; their usability hinges entirely on support retrieval, currently unprincipled.
why_possibly_novel: Support-retrieval law-fitting for dense in-context learning is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Sweep support choice along controlled similarity axes on in-context segmenters, fit gain predictors, validate learned retrieval on held-out tasks.
main_risk: Laws may be model-specific; test across 2-3 in-context architectures.

one_liner: When does nearest-neighbor label transfer beat fine-tuning? Map the regime boundary for non-parametric segmentation over foundation features.
problem: With strong frozen features, segmenting by retrieving similar labeled patches and transferring their labels (non-parametric) competes with parametric fine-tuning. The regime map - along labeled-set size, domain shift, and class granularity - of which paradigm wins where has not been drawn.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: nearest-neighbor transfer dominates fine-tuning below a measurable labeled-data threshold (a few hundred masks) and under moderate shift (retrieval adapts instance-wise; parameters overfit), while fine-tuning wins on fine-grained class boundaries requiring feature reshaping - and the crossover locations are predictable from feature-space class separability statistics, giving practitioners a measurement-driven paradigm selector.
why_important: The low-label regime is where most real projects start; knowing when to skip training entirely (retrieval only) saves widespread wasted effort.
why_possibly_novel: Paradigm regime-mapping with predictive crossover is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Grid over labeled-set size x shift x granularity comparing kNN-transfer vs fine-tuning on frozen DINOv2/SAM features, fit crossover predictors.
main_risk: kNN implementation quality (feature aggregation, spatial priors) strongly affects the frontier; use well-tuned versions of both paradigms.

one_liner: Resolution extrapolation failures are radially structured: positional-encoding interpolation breaks dense prediction from the image border inward.
problem: Models trained at low resolution are deployed at high resolution via positional-embedding interpolation; failures are treated as uniform degradation, but interpolation error geometry (extrapolation at borders, compression at center) predicts spatially structured damage nobody has mapped.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: under resolution extrapolation, dense-prediction error increases with a characteristic radial profile (worst at borders and corners, tracking positional-embedding interpolation error), the profile shape is predictable from the embedding scheme (learned absolute vs RoPE-style vs conv-derived), and border-cropped evaluation recovers most of the reported extrapolation gap - 'resolution generalization failure' is substantially a positional-geometry artifact with scheme-specific signatures.
why_important: Correct attribution changes the fix (positional scheme surgery, not retraining) and warns that border-heavy applications (panorama, document edges) suffer most.
why_possibly_novel: Radial error-profiling of resolution extrapolation is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Evaluate models across resolution ladders, map spatial error profiles per positional scheme, test border-crop recovery predictions.
main_risk: Content statistics also vary radially in photos (center bias); control with content-shuffled synthetic layouts.

one_liner: Do vision foundations share an object space? Measure cross-model representational alignment specifically on object-level axes, not global features.
problem: The platonic-representation debate (do independently trained models converge?) has been argued with global similarity metrics (KNOWN: representational-alignment literature exists); whether alignment holds specifically for OBJECT-level structure (boundaries, part decompositions, instance separations) - the part dense prediction cares about - is finer-grained and unresolved.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: object-level alignment between foundations (measured by transferability of object-axis linear maps between SAM/DINOv2/CLIP feature spaces) is substantially higher than global feature alignment, alignment grows with each model's downstream dense performance (convergence tracks competence), and residual misalignment localizes to specific properties (part granularity, boundary ownership) that differ by pretraining objective - the ecosystem is converging on WHAT objects are but not on their decomposition.
why_important: Convergence structure determines whether ensembling/stitching pays and what unique value each pretraining lineage retains - portfolio-level strategy for the field.
why_possibly_novel: Object-axis-resolved alignment measurement is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Fit cross-model linear maps on object-centric probe tasks, quantify transfer per property, correlate alignment with performance across checkpoint ladders.
main_risk: Alignment metrics are subtle (CKA critiques are KNOWN); use multiple alignment measures and behavioral (not just geometric) tests.

one_liner: Vocabulary is a confounder in open-vocabulary segmentation: performance depends on distractor-list composition as much as on the model - benchmark the benchmark.
problem: Open-vocabulary segmentation scores depend on the evaluation vocabulary (which distractor classes compete), yet benchmarks fix arbitrary small vocabularies, making cross-paper numbers incomparable and inflating apparent competence relative to open-world deployment with thousands of candidate labels.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: OV segmentation scores decay predictably with vocabulary size and semantic density (distractor proximity), model RANKINGS flip between small-vocabulary and large-vocabulary regimes (some models are precision-optimized, others recall-optimized), and reporting vocabulary-scaling CURVES instead of point scores restores comparability - one protocol fix rescuing an incoherent evaluation ecosystem.
why_important: OV segmentation is the field's deployment-facing product; incomparable evaluation blocks real progress assessment.
why_possibly_novel: Vocabulary-scaling evaluation protocol with rank-flip demonstration is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Evaluate 6 OV models across controlled vocabulary ladders (size x density), demonstrate rank instability, propose and validate curve-based reporting.
main_risk: Overlaps conceptually with confidence-dilution idea (W2-A-0197) but targets evaluation protocol rather than confidence mechanics; keep both with distinct deliverables.

one_liner: How small can a decoder be? Localize where dense-task capacity actually lives by scaling decoders down over frozen foundations.
problem: Dense architectures allocate large decoders by convention, but if frozen foundation features already contain the needed information, decoder capacity might shrink drastically without loss - the capacity-localization question (encoder vs decoder) has never been answered with systematic decoder-scaling curves.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: over strong frozen encoders, segmentation performance vs decoder size shows a sharp knee at surprisingly small capacity (<1% of encoder parameters) for region metrics, but boundary metrics keep improving with decoder size (boundary computation genuinely lives in the decoder), and the knee position shifts predictably with encoder quality - a capacity-localization law separating what encoders know from what decoders compute.
why_important: Design efficiency (edge deployment) plus scientific attribution: knowing where each output property is computed directs both compression and improvement efforts.
why_possibly_novel: Property-resolved decoder-scaling laws are UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Decoder-size ladders over 3 frozen foundations x 3 datasets, fit property-resolved capacity curves, locate knees vs encoder quality.
main_risk: Decoder architecture family may matter as much as size; replicate across 2 families.

one_liner: How precisely can MLLMs localize without a pixel decoder? Measure the text-coordinate segmentation ceiling of GPT-4V-class models.
problem: Multimodal LLMs describe and point at image content via text coordinates (boxes, polygon vertices as numbers). Their intrinsic localization precision - the ceiling of language-emitted geometry - determines whether pixel decoders are necessary or just convenient, and it has not been carefully measured.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: MLLM text-coordinate boundary precision plateaus around coarse levels (5-10% of object scale) regardless of prompt engineering (a representation bottleneck, not an interface artifact - verifiable by probing whether visual tokens contain finer position information than the text head extracts), implying pixel-space readouts are structurally required for boundary tasks while detection-grade localization is already language-achievable.
why_important: Architectural guidance for the merging of MLLMs and dense vision: what must be grafted on versus what emerges from scale.
why_possibly_novel: Ceiling measurement with internal-information comparison (tokens vs text head) is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Elicit coordinate outputs from 4 MLLMs across precision-demanding tasks, compare against linear probes on their visual tokens for the same geometry.
main_risk: Closed-model probing is limited; use open MLLMs for the internal-information leg.

one_liner: Does a granularity dial exist in prompt space? Search for a continuous direction controlling part-object-group level in promptable segmenters.
problem: SAM's granularity is controlled crudely (multimask choice); whether the underlying prompt-embedding space contains a continuous, monotonic granularity direction (allowing smooth part-to-whole dialing) is a concrete representational geometry question with direct interface value.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a single direction in SAM's prompt-token space monotonically controls output granularity across categories (found via paired part/whole supervision on a small set, transferring zero-shot to unseen categories), demonstrating granularity is linearly represented - and its transferability failure cases (categories with non-nested part structures) reveal where object decomposition is genuinely non-hierarchical.
why_important: A working dial would fix promptable segmentation's most common practical failure (wrong granularity), and the geometry finding informs how composition is encoded.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-space granularity-direction search is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Fit granularity directions on part-annotated categories (PACO/PartImageNet), test zero-shot transfer, characterize monotonicity and failure taxonomy.
main_risk: Granularity may be encoded nonlinearly or per-category; a negative result still maps the encoding structure.

one_liner: Trace a bad mask to its training data: feasibility of influence-function attribution for promptable segmentation failures.
problem: When SAM fails on a mask, nobody can say WHICH training data (or absence thereof) is responsible - data attribution methods exist for classification (KNOWN: influence functions, TracIn lineage) but their feasibility, cost, and validity for billion-mask promptable models is untested.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: scalable attribution approximations (gradient-sketch retrieval over training shards) identify training-set regions whose removal/addition causally changes specific failure behaviors (validated by targeted fine-tuning on attributed shards fixing the failure at above-random rates), making failure-driven data curation - fix the model by editing data, not weights - a practical loop for segmentation foundations.
why_important: Data curation is the main lever for foundation model quality; closing the failure-to-data loop would industrialize it.
why_possibly_novel: Attribution-driven repair loops for dense foundations are UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: On an open SAM-scale-down reproduction, attribute 100 failure cases, run targeted-data interventions, measure repair rates vs random-data controls.
main_risk: Attribution approximations may be too noisy at scale; the scaled-down setting bounds feasibility honestly.

one_liner: Shared blind spots across the model zoo: pixels where ALL foundations fail mark data-ecosystem holes, not architecture limits.
problem: Per-model error analysis cannot distinguish 'this architecture's weakness' from 'nobody's training data covers this'. Cross-model failure correlation - the shared-vs-unique error decomposition across independent lineages - has never been systematically computed for dense prediction.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: a large fraction of segmentation errors (>40%) are shared across architecturally-independent models (data-ecosystem holes: web-photo biases, absent domains), shared-error regions are predictable from data-frequency estimates (how rare such pixels are online), and unique errors cluster by architectural family - producing an actionable split: fix shared errors with data expeditions, unique errors with architecture work.
why_important: The field's error-fixing effort is misallocated without this decomposition; shared holes need collection campaigns no single lab's method work can fill.
why_possibly_novel: Ecosystem-level error-correlation decomposition is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Run 10 diverse models on 5 benchmarks, decompose per-pixel error correlation, correlate shared-error regions with web-frequency proxies.
main_risk: Lineage independence is eroding (shared data everywhere); quantify lineage overlap as a covariate.

one_liner: Image pretraining plus explicit tracking versus native video pretraining: budget-matched showdown for dense video tasks.
problem: Video foundation models cost far more to train than image models; whether native temporal pretraining buys anything over strong image features composed with lightweight tracking machinery - at matched total budget - is the central economics question of video representation learning, never cleanly tested.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: for video segmentation tasks dominated by appearance continuity, image-pretraining + tracking matches or beats native video pretraining at equal budget (temporal structure is cheap to add post hoc), but a specific task subset (occlusion reasoning, motion-defined objects, temporal event boundaries) shows irreducible native-video advantages - defining precisely WHICH temporal capabilities require temporal pretraining and which do not.
why_important: Directly prices the video-pretraining premium and would redirect large compute investments if the composed alternative suffices for most tasks.
why_possibly_novel: Budget-matched composed-vs-native comparison with capability decomposition is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Match total budgets between (image SSL + tracking head) and video SSL pipelines, evaluate across a task battery stratified by temporal-dependence, itemize where native wins.
main_risk: Budget matching across paradigms has degrees of freedom; pre-register the accounting rules.

one_liner: Can a segmentation foundation be trained on zero real images? Push procedural-data pretraining (fractals, formulas, simulations) to its dense-prediction limit.
problem: Formula/fractal pretraining works surprisingly well for classification (KNOWN: FractalDB line of work exists); whether procedurally-generated data - with its perfect free labels and zero licensing/privacy burden - can carry DENSE pretraining to competitive levels, and what procedural ingredients matter, is largely unmapped.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: procedural pretraining reaches a substantial fraction (>70%) of real-data pretraining transfer for segmentation IF the generator includes specific ingredients - occlusion layering, boundary-complexity distributions matched to natural statistics, and material-like texture gradients - and ingredient ablations identify occlusion structure as the single most transfer-critical property, revealing what dense pretraining actually needs from data (compositional structure, not semantics).
why_important: A viable real-image-free pretraining path solves licensing/privacy constraints (medical!) and scientifically isolates which data properties dense learning consumes.
why_possibly_novel: Ingredient-ablated procedural pretraining for dense tasks is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search beyond the KNOWN classification-focused work.
minimal_experiment: Build parameterized procedural generator, pretrain matched models across ingredient ablations, measure segmentation transfer against real-data controls.
main_risk: The gap may be irreducible for semantic tasks; even so, the ingredient-importance map is standalone valuable.

one_liner: Compression kills boundaries first: quantization and distillation degrade dense outputs in a property-ordered sequence worth mapping.
problem: Model compression is validated on aggregate metrics, but dense-output properties (region semantics, boundary precision, small-object recall, calibration) may degrade at very different rates - the degradation ORDER determines which applications can use compressed models, and it is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: across compression methods (quantization, pruning, distillation), dense properties degrade in a consistent order - boundary precision first, small-object recall second, region semantics last (mirroring their dependence on high-frequency feature content) - and the ordering enables property-targeted compression (protecting boundary-critical channels identified by sensitivity analysis) that shifts the frontier for boundary-dependent applications.
why_important: Edge deployment of segmentation is exploding; property-ordered degradation maps tell each application what compression it can afford.
why_possibly_novel: Property-resolved compression analysis for dense prediction is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Compress 3 segmentation models along method ladders, track property-resolved metrics, test the protection scheme on boundary-critical channels.
main_risk: Ordering may vary by architecture; establish across families before claiming universality.

one_liner: Decode what learned dense prompts encode: continuous prompt vectors trained for segmentation tasks are interpretable dataset fingerprints.
problem: Visual prompt tuning learns small parameter sets that adapt frozen models to datasets; these vectors must encode the dataset's distinctive properties (class priors, boundary conventions, granularity), but nobody has tried to READ them - an interpretability opportunity with practical payoffs (dataset similarity, transfer prediction).
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: learned dense-task prompts are decodable - prompt-space distances between datasets predict cross-dataset transfer performance (prompt geometry is a transfer map), prompt arithmetic works (combining prompts of dataset A's classes with dataset B's boundary convention), and specific prompt components isolate annotation-convention information - making prompts both a scientific instrument for dataset comparison and an engineering tool for convention translation.
why_important: A working dataset-fingerprint algebra would answer 'how similar are these datasets' and 'will transfer work' from cheap artifacts instead of expensive experiments.
why_possibly_novel: Prompt-space decoding and arithmetic for dense tasks is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Train prompts across 12 datasets on one frozen foundation, test distance-transfer correlation and convention-swap arithmetic on held-out pairs.
main_risk: Prompt solutions are non-unique (different seeds, same behavior); test geometry stability across seeds first.

one_liner: Is promptable segmentation emergent or smooth? Train a mini-SAM scaling series and settle whether the capability has a threshold.
problem: Emergence debates (capabilities appearing suddenly at scale) are unresolved for dense prediction: does promptability - responding correctly to spatial prompts - develop smoothly with scale or exhibit threshold behavior? The SAM training recipe at reduced scales provides a clean testbed nobody has exploited.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: prompt-following ability measured with fine-grained metrics develops SMOOTHLY across a mini-SAM scaling series (no emergence - apparent thresholds in prior anecdotes are metric artifacts, consistent with the KNOWN emergence-as-metric-artifact critique in LLMs), but specific sub-capabilities (negative-prompt understanding, multi-prompt integration) show genuinely delayed development - a capability-resolved developmental timeline for promptable vision.
why_important: Whether capabilities emerge or accrue determines training-investment risk (can you extrapolate from small pilots?) - a first-order question for anyone training dense foundations.
why_possibly_novel: Scaling-series developmental analysis of promptability is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Train 6 SAM-recipe models from tiny to small scale on SA-1B subsets, evaluate capability-resolved prompt-following curves with continuous metrics.
main_risk: Mini-scale conclusions may not extrapolate to frontier scale; frame as developmental science with stated bounds.

one_liner: Feature quality is spatially anisotropic: foundation features degrade toward image borders, and panoramic/tiled applications inherit the damage.
problem: Foundation features are treated as spatially homogeneous, but training photos have strong center bias (subjects centered, borders contain periphery), plausibly training center-privileged features - a spatial quality gradient that tiled inference and panorama processing would repeatedly sample at its worst.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: probing tasks show systematic center-to-border feature quality gradients across foundations (matched-content probes decoding worse near borders), the gradient magnitude tracks each training corpus's measured center bias (data-borne, not architectural), and tiling strategies that avoid placing content at tile borders recover measurable accuracy in tiled high-resolution inference - a hidden spatial prior with direct engineering consequences.
why_important: Tiled inference is universal for high-res imagery (satellite, pathology); an unrecognized border penalty means widespread silent quality loss with a cheap layout fix.
why_possibly_novel: Spatial feature-quality gradient measurement is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Probe matched content at controlled positions across foundations, correlate gradients with corpus center-bias statistics, benchmark border-aware tiling.
main_risk: Positional embeddings entangle with content statistics; use content-controlled synthetic placements.

one_liner: Object tokens or distributed objectness? Causal feature-surgery to locate WHERE promptable models represent each object.
problem: Whether SAM-style models maintain discrete object-centric representations (tokens 'owning' objects) or distributed objectness (objects as patterns over patch features) is a resolvable representational question - via causal intervention (ablate/swap candidate representations, observe mask behavior) rather than correlational probing.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: causal interventions will show object identity is carried by a low-rank subspace of the mask-token pathway (swapping it transfers masks between objects; ablating it deletes specific objects while preserving scene features) - promptable models ARE object-centric in a strong causal sense, and the object subspace's dimensionality measures how many objects the model can simultaneously individuate (predicting multi-object interference limits).
why_important: Resolves a foundational representation question with a measurable capacity constant (simultaneous-object limit) that predicts practical failure in crowded scenes.
why_possibly_novel: Causal object-representation surgery on promptable segmenters is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Implement token/subspace swap-and-ablate interventions on SAM's decoder pathway, quantify mask-transfer and deletion specificity, estimate object-subspace rank.
main_risk: Interventions may push activations off-manifold, producing artifacts misread as structure; use manifold-constrained interventions.

one_liner: Transformers' low-frequency bias caps boundary precision architecturally: same-data CNN-vs-ViT boundary spectroscopy.
problem: Spectral-bias theory says different architectures preferentially learn different frequency bands; boundary precision is a high-frequency output property, so architecture-level frequency bias should produce measurable boundary-quality differences at matched data and training - a clean theory-to-practice test never run for segmentation.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: at matched data/compute/parameters, boundary-error spectra (error energy vs spatial frequency along contours) show architecture-specific cutoffs consistent with spectral-bias theory (ViTs attenuate high-frequency boundary detail more than CNNs at equal aggregate mIoU), the difference persists across scale, and hybrid stems (conv early, attention late) inherit the CNN cutoff - architecture choice imposes a measurable boundary-frequency ceiling independent of learning.
why_important: Would ground the CNN-vs-ViT debate in a measurable, property-specific law rather than aggregate benchmarks, guiding architecture choice for boundary-critical applications.
why_possibly_novel: Boundary-spectral architecture comparison at matched budgets is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Train matched CNN/ViT/hybrid segmenters on identical data, compute boundary error spectra (using the physical-GT stimuli for precision), compare cutoffs.
main_risk: Matched training across architecture families is never perfectly fair; sweep learning configurations and report robustness.

one_liner: Segmentation as retrieval at scale: how does non-parametric mask transfer scale with memory size, and does it ever beat parametric knowledge?
problem: A segmentation system could store millions of labeled region exemplars and segment by retrieval+transfer, scaling knowledge by growing memory rather than retraining - the scaling behavior of memory size versus parametric capacity for dense tasks (retrieval's sweet spots, its ceiling) is uncharted.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: retrieval-based segmentation accuracy scales log-linearly with memory size well past the point where matched-parameter models plateau (memory beats parameters for tail classes and rare configurations), with retrieval's advantage concentrated in the frequency tail while parametric models retain the head - implying optimal systems are frequency-split hybrids, and the crossover frequency is measurable and stable.
why_important: Memory-augmented architectures are rising everywhere else (LLM RAG); establishing the dense-prediction scaling equivalent would guide the next architecture generation.
why_possibly_novel: Memory-scaling laws for dense prediction are UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Build exemplar-memory segmenter over frozen features, scale memory across orders of magnitude, compare per-frequency-bin against parametric models at matched total footprint.
main_risk: Retrieval latency and memory engineering may dominate practicality; the science stands regardless of deployment economics.

one_liner: If all strong models converge, ensembles die: test whether dense-model ensemble gains are collapsing generation by generation.
problem: Ensembling assumes error diversity; if foundation-era models increasingly share data, objectives, and representations (monoculture convergence), ensemble gains should be measurably shrinking over model generations - a trend with major implications that nobody has tracked.
core_hypothesis: HYPOTHESIS: measuring ensemble gain (over best member) across model cohorts by era shows monotonic decline for dense tasks (error-diversity collapse as lineages share SA-1B/LAION-descended data), the decline is steeper than in the classification ecosystem (dense labels are scarcer, forcing more sharing), and remaining diversity concentrates in models with genuinely disjoint data (medical vs web) - quantifying the ecosystem's convergence tax on reliability engineering.
why_important: Safety-critical systems rely on ensembling/redundancy; if diversity is evaporating ecosystem-wide, redundancy-based safety arguments weaken - better to know now, with numbers.
why_possibly_novel: Longitudinal ensemble-gain trend analysis is UNVERIFIED - needs lit search.
minimal_experiment: Assemble model cohorts by era (2019-2025), measure ensemble gains and error correlations on fixed benchmarks, regress against lineage-overlap measures.
main_risk: Era confounds with scale and performance level; normalize gains by member accuracy and test scale-matched cohorts.
